titans.name: Isaac Newton
titans.tagline: Invented calculus because he was bored during a plague. You learned to bake banana bread.
titans.quote: If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.
titans.quoteContext: Said this to Robert Hooke, who was short. Probably shade.
powerMoves: Invented calculus — independently, during a pandemic, in his 20s, as a side project
Laws of motion — three rules that govern literally everything you can see
Universal gravitation — watched an apple fall and figured out why the Moon doesn't
Built the first reflecting telescope — got bored of chromatic aberration
Wrote the Principia — arguably the most important book in the history of science
titans.funFact: Stuck a needle behind his own eyeball to study optics. Also ran the Royal Mint and personally hunted down counterfeiters. Went hard at everything.
tea: Reportedly died a virgin. The man who described the fundamental forces of the universe may never have experienced the most basic human one.
Tried to erase Robert Hooke from history — when Newton became president of the Royal Society, Hooke's only known portrait conveniently 'disappeared.' It has never been found.

Spent more of his life on alchemy and biblical chronology than on physics. His unpublished writings on the occult outweigh his scientific work by a factor of ten. The father of modern science was, privately, a medieval mystic.

Had a full nervous breakdown in 1693, possibly from mercury poisoning during his alchemy experiments. Sent paranoid, accusatory letters to friends. The price of sticking needles in your eye and inhaling mercury fumes.
rivalries: Robert Hooke (gravity beef, optics beef, just general beef)

media.title: But what is the Fourier Transform? — 3Blue1Brown

titans.name: Albert Einstein
titans.tagline: Patent clerk who casually rewrote the fabric of reality on his lunch breaks.
titans.quote: Imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world.
titans.quoteContext: From a 1929 interview. He was not kidding.
powerMoves: Special relativity (1905) — time is not what you think it is
General relativity (1915) — space is not what you think it is either
Photoelectric effect — won the Nobel for this, not relativity, because the committee couldn't handle it
Mass-energy equivalence — four letters, one equation, everything changed
Brownian motion — proved atoms exist, casually, in the same year as relativity
titans.funFact: 1905 is called his 'Annus Mirabilis' — he published four papers that each would have been career-defining. He published them all in one year. While working full-time at a patent office. He was 26.
tea: Had multiple affairs while married. His relationship with a Soviet spy, Margarita Konenkova, was discovered decades later through love letters auctioned in 1998. The man who understood the universe couldn't figure out discretion.

Married his first cousin Elsa. She was also his second cousin on his mother's side. He reportedly chose her over her daughter — Elsa's own daughter Ilse — who he'd also considered. The family tree gets complicated.
His first wife Mileva agreed to divorce only after he promised her his future Nobel Prize money. He agreed. He won. She got the money. The most expensive physics prediction ever made.

Drew up a contract for Mileva that included rules like 'you will stop talking to me if I request it' and 'you will not expect any intimacy from me.' He framed the fabric of spacetime but couldn't frame a healthy relationship.
Abandoned his first daughter Lieserl — born before his marriage to Mileva. Her fate remains unknown. The man who solved the mysteries of the universe left one of his own.
rivalries: Niels Bohr (the quantum debate — Einstein kept losing and refused to accept it)

media.title: Why No One Has Measured The Speed Of Light — Veritasium
General Relativity Explained — PBS Space Time

titans.name: Leonhard Euler
titans.tagline: The most prolific mathematician in history. Went blind. Didn't slow down. Output actually increased.
titans.quote: Read Euler, read Euler, he is the master of us all.
titans.quoteContext: — Pierre-Simon Laplace. Even other geniuses were fanboys.
powerMoves: Euler's identity — five fundamental constants, one equation, mathematicians literally weep
Graph theory — solved the Seven Bridges of Konigsberg and invented a field
Euler's formula for polyhedra — V - E + F = 2, simple, beautiful, everywhere
Pioneered calculus of variations, number theory, and topology — before lunch apparently
Published 866 papers and books — a record that stood for over a century
titans.funFact: Lost vision in his right eye at 28, went fully blind at 59. His mathematical output doubled after going blind because he could finally concentrate without distractions. Absolute unit.
rivalries: Daniel Bernoulli (friendly but intense mathematical competition)

titans.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
titans.tagline: The 'Prince of Mathematicians.' Discovered things, didn't bother publishing, then got annoyed when others discovered them later.
titans.quote: Mathematics is the queen of the sciences and number theory is the queen of mathematics.
titans.quoteContext: He meant it. Number theory was his favorite child and he didn't hide it.
powerMoves: Summed 1 to 100 instantly — age 7, in class, to spite his teacher
Proved the fundamental theorem of algebra — his PhD thesis, done properly
Gaussian distribution — the bell curve, named after him, used by literally everyone
Non-Euclidean geometry — figured it out decades before anyone else, didn't publish because he didn't want the drama
Invented the heliotrope and the magnetometer — physics was his side hustle
titans.funFact: When told his infant son was dying, reportedly said 'Please tell my wife to wait a moment, I'm almost done' while working on a proof. The quote may be apocryphal but the fact that people believed it tells you everything.
tea: Discovered non-Euclidean geometry years before Bolyai and Lobachevsky but refused to publish because he feared ridicule. When Bolyai's father sent him the son's paper, Gauss replied that praising it would mean 'praising myself.' Bolyai was devastated and never published again. Gauss's fear of controversy cost another mathematician his career.

Had a terrible relationship with his sons. One emigrated to America partly to escape his father's shadow. Gauss reportedly showed more emotion toward a mathematical proof than toward his own children. The prince of mathematics was a commoner of fatherhood.
rivalries: No one. He was too far ahead. His only rival was his own filing cabinet of unpublished results.

media.title: Gauss: The Prince of Mathematics — Mathologer
How Gauss Determined the Date of Easter — Numberphile

titans.name: James Clerk Maxwell
titans.tagline: Unified electricity, magnetism, and light into four equations. Einstein kept his photo on his wall. Enough said.
titans.quote: What is done by what is called myself is, I feel, done by something greater than myself in me.
titans.quoteContext: Humble to a fault. The man who unified electromagnetism thought he was just along for the ride.
powerMoves: Maxwell's equations — four equations that describe all electromagnetic phenomena. All of it.
Predicted electromagnetic waves — then Hertz proved him right, then we got radio, TV, wifi, everything
First color photograph — yes, he did that too, in 1861
Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution — co-founded statistical mechanics for fun
Proved Saturn's rings must be particles — won the Adams Prize at Cambridge
titans.funFact: Einstein was once asked what it felt like to be the smartest person alive. He replied: 'I don't know, you'll have to ask Maxwell.' (Maxwell was already dead by then. Einstein still said it.)
rivalries: Lord Kelvin (who kept insisting Maxwell's theory was wrong — it wasn't)

media.title: The Most Important Equations in Physics — Domain of Science

titans.name: Richard Feynman
titans.tagline: The Great Explainer. Cracked safes at Los Alamos for fun. Played bongo drums. Won a Nobel.
titans.quote: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.
titans.quoteContext: From his Caltech commencement address. Delivered with the energy of a man who also cracked safes for fun.
powerMoves: Feynman diagrams — turned quantum field theory into pictures that actually make sense
Path integral formulation — reimagined all of quantum mechanics from scratch
Quantum electrodynamics (QED) — the most precisely tested theory in all of science
Challenger investigation — dunked an O-ring in ice water on live TV to prove NASA wrong
The Feynman Lectures — three volumes that made physics accessible to mortals
titans.funFact: During the Manhattan Project, he learned to crack safes and would leave notes in classified filing cabinets saying 'Guess who?' Security was not amused. Feynman was extremely amused.
tea: Wrote candidly about learning to pick up women at bars using calculated psychological tactics. Documented the whole system in 'Surely You're Joking.' The man who systematized quantum electrodynamics also tried to systematize seduction.

Frequented strip clubs in Pasadena and did physics on napkins there. Caltech was not thrilled. Feynman did not care. The line between 'eccentric genius' and 'HR liability' was thinner than a Feynman diagram.

His second wife, Mary Louise Bell, cited 'cruelty' in their divorce after two years. She said living with him was like 'living with a whirlwind.' The man who made physics fun to learn was apparently less fun to live with.
rivalries: Murray Gell-Mann (office neighbors at Caltech, intellectual frenemies, both won Nobels)

media.title: The Character of Physical Law — Feynman

titans.name: Emmy Noether
titans.tagline: The most important mathematician most people have never heard of. Einstein called her a genius. She was.
titans.quote: My methods are really methods of working and thinking; this is why they have crept in everywhere anonymously.
titans.quoteContext: Her ideas were so fundamental they became invisible — baked into the fabric of modern physics.
powerMoves: Noether's theorem — every symmetry in physics has a conservation law. Revolutionized everything.
Abstract algebra — basically invented the modern version of it
Proved that conservation of energy comes from time symmetry — mic drop for all of physics
Ring theory, ideal theory — foundational structures that all of modern algebra uses
Did all of this while being barred from official university positions because she was a woman
titans.funFact: Was not allowed to teach at Gottingen under her own name. Hilbert listed her courses under his name and told the faculty senate: 'I do not see that the sex of the candidate is an argument against her admission. After all, we are a university, not a bath house.'
tea: Fled Nazi Germany in 1933 after being dismissed from her position for being Jewish. Ended up at Bryn Mawr in Pennsylvania. Einstein wrote her New York Times obituary and called her 'the most significant creative mathematical genius thus far produced since the higher education of women began.' She died two years after arriving, at 53.

Lived for mathematics so completely that colleagues described her personal life as essentially nonexistent. Not as a tragedy — she genuinely seemed to prefer theorems to everything else. The system kept telling her she couldn't do math. She decided math was all she would do.
rivalries: The entire German university system (she won)

media.title: The Most Beautiful Theorem in Physics — Looking Glass Universe

titans.name: Paul Dirac
titans.tagline: Predicted antimatter exists by staring at an equation and refusing to ignore the negative solution. Barely spoke. Didn't need to.
titans.quote: In science one tries to tell people, in such a way as to be understood by everyone, something that no one ever knew before.
titans.quoteContext: Ironic coming from a man famously described as having 'no social skills whatsoever.'
powerMoves: The Dirac equation — unified quantum mechanics and special relativity in one stroke
Predicted antimatter — the equation had a 'negative energy' solution. Everyone said ignore it. He said no. He was right.
Dirac delta function — not technically a function. Mathematicians were furious. Physicists loved it.
Quantum field theory foundations — co-created the framework for all of particle physics
Won the Nobel at 31 — considered declining it because he didn't want the publicity
titans.funFact: His colleagues at Cambridge defined a unit of measurement called the 'dirac' — one word per hour. When Heisenberg went dancing at a conference, Dirac asked: 'Why do you dance?' Heisenberg said: 'It's pleasant to dance with nice girls.' Dirac replied: 'But how do you know beforehand that the girls are nice?'
tea: Said his father's death was 'the greatest liberation of my life.' His father, a Swiss-born French teacher, enforced a rule: Paul could only eat dinner with him if he spoke exclusively in French. Any mistake and he was sent away. Dirac later attributed his legendary silence to this — he learned that speaking leads to punishment.
Married the sister of his colleague Eugene Wigner. When asked how it happened, he reportedly said he'd been looking for someone quiet. The courtship was apparently as efficient as his equations.

media.title: The Dirac Equation — Looking Glass Universe

titans.name: Alan Turing
titans.tagline: Invented the concept of the computer, broke Nazi encryption, was thanked with criminal prosecution. Humanity's greatest L.
titans.quote: Sometimes it is the people no one imagines anything of who do the things that no one can imagine.
titans.quoteContext: Attributed. Whether he said it or not, it's the truest thing ever written about him.
powerMoves: The Turing machine (1936) — a theoretical device that defined computation itself, before computers existed
Broke Enigma — cracked the Nazi cipher machine, shortened WWII by an estimated 2 years, saved millions of lives
The Turing test — proposed the foundational question of artificial intelligence
Morphogenesis paper — explained how biological patterns form. Published in 1952. Still cited.
Basically invented computer science — as a concept, as a field, as a thing
titans.funFact: Was an elite marathon runner with a personal best of 2:46:03 — good enough to nearly qualify for the 1948 Olympics. He used running to deal with stress. The man who invented computing was also almost an Olympian.
tea: Prosecuted in 1952 for 'gross indecency' — being gay. Given a choice between prison and chemical castration. He chose the hormones. The man who saved millions of lives by breaking Enigma was rewarded by the state with forced estrogen injections.

Died of cyanide poisoning in 1954, a half-eaten apple beside his bed. The inquest ruled suicide, but his mother insisted it was accidental — he was careless with chemicals. The apple was never tested. Some have speculated the Apple logo is a tribute, but the company denies it.

His work at Bletchley Park was classified for decades. He died without the public knowing he'd helped win the war. The British government didn't officially apologize until 2009. The royal pardon came in 2013. Fifty-nine years too late for a man already dead.
rivalries: The British government (which prosecuted him for being gay, then apologized 59 years too late)

titans.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
titans.tagline: Self-taught genius from Madras who mailed his theorems to Cambridge. Hardy rated him a 100 out of 100. Hardy rated himself a 25.
titans.quote: An equation for me has no meaning unless it expresses a thought of God.
titans.quoteContext: He was not being metaphorical. He credited his mathematical visions to the goddess Namagiri.
powerMoves: The Ramanujan conjecture — proved to be connected to the deepest structures in mathematics
Hardy-Ramanujan number (1729) — 'the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.' He noticed this about a taxi number. Casually.
Mock theta functions — invented on his deathbed. Mathematicians are STILL unpacking them 100 years later
Infinite series for pi — his formulas are used in modern supercomputer calculations
Produced 3,900 results — most without formal proofs, most later proven correct
titans.funFact: Mailed unsolicited theorems to G.H. Hardy at Cambridge. Hardy initially thought it was a crank letter, then realized it contained results that were decades ahead of current mathematics. Hardy said discovering Ramanujan was 'the one romantic incident in my life.'
tea: A devout Hindu vegetarian stranded in wartime England where rationing meant almost nothing he could eat was available. His health deteriorated partly from malnutrition. The country that gave him a platform also starved him slowly. He went home to India to recover and died at 32.

His wife Janaki was largely erased from his story for decades. She was 10 when they married (an arranged marriage, common in the era). After his death, she fought for decades to get recognition and a pension. The mathematical community celebrated her husband's genius while ignoring the woman he left behind.
rivalries: Formal mathematical proofs (he considered them optional)

media.title: Ramanujan: The Man Who Knew Infinity — Numberphile

titans.name: Stephen Hawking
titans.tagline: Told he had two years to live at 21. Proceeded to rewrite our understanding of the universe for the next 55.
titans.quote: Not only does God play dice, but He sometimes throws them where they cannot be seen.
titans.quoteContext: A direct response to Einstein's famous 'God does not play dice.' Hawking was not impressed by Einstein's quantum hangups.
powerMoves: Hawking radiation — black holes aren't completely black. They glow. This unified quantum mechanics and general relativity for the first time.
Singularity theorems (with Penrose) — proved the Big Bang was a real singularity, not just a mathematical artifact
A Brief History of Time — sold 25 million copies. A book about cosmology. On the bestseller list for 237 weeks.
Black hole information paradox — posed a problem so deep that physicists are still fighting about it
Proved black holes have entropy — thermodynamics applies even at the edge of spacetime
titans.funFact: Placed a bet with Kip Thorne that Cygnus X-1 was NOT a black hole — even though his own work suggested it was. He called it 'insurance.' If black holes didn't exist, at least he'd win the bet (a magazine subscription). He lost. Happily.
tea: Left his wife Jane after 25 years for his nurse, Elaine Mason. Jane's memoir 'Travelling to Infinity' didn't hold back — she described years of feeling invisible next to his celebrity. The man who explained black holes created a kind of gravitational pull that consumed the people closest to him.

Visited strip clubs and was reportedly a regular at Stringfellows in London. When the press found out, his office didn't deny it. The world's most famous physicist in a wheelchair at a strip club is either a scandal or the most human thing imaginable, depending on your perspective.

His fame created a paradox: the public saw a heroic mind trapped in a failing body, but those closest to him described someone who could be cold, controlling, and fully aware of his power. The simplified narrative was always more comfortable than the complicated human.
rivalries: Leonard Susskind (the black hole information war — lasted decades, Hawking eventually conceded)

media.title: A Brief History of Time — documentary

titans.name: Marie Curie
titans.tagline: Won two Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her notebooks are still too radioactive to handle without protective equipment.
titans.quote: Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood. Now is the time to understand more, so that we may fear less.
titans.quoteContext: Said by a woman who literally carried test tubes of radium in her pockets.
powerMoves: Discovered polonium AND radium — named one after her homeland, because she never forgot where she came from
First woman to win a Nobel Prize — then won a second one, in a different field, just to be safe
Pioneered mobile X-ray units in WWI — drove them to the front lines herself. They called them 'petites Curies.'
Coined the term 'radioactivity' — named the phenomenon she discovered
First woman professor at the Sorbonne — took over her dead husband's position and immediately surpassed his work
titans.funFact: Her personal effects — including her cookbook — are stored in lead-lined boxes at the Bibliotheque nationale de France. You need to sign a liability waiver and wear protective clothing to view them. She's been dead for 90 years. Her stuff is still hot.
tea: After Pierre died, she had an affair with Paul Langevin — a married physicist and former student of Pierre's. His wife leaked their love letters to the press. The French tabloids called Marie a 'foreign Jewish home-wrecker' (she was neither Jewish nor the one who was married). She nearly lost her second Nobel over it.

The Nobel committee asked her not to come to Stockholm to accept her second prize because of the scandal. She came anyway. Collected it. Went home. The committee learned that Marie Curie did not take direction well.

Carried test tubes of radium in her coat pockets and stored them in her desk drawer because she liked the pretty blue glow. The woman who named radioactivity had essentially no concept of radiation safety. Her death from aplastic anemia was almost certainly caused by decades of casual exposure to the thing she discovered.
rivalries: The French Academy of Sciences (refused to admit her because she was a woman — she had two Nobels at that point)

titans.name: Ludwig Boltzmann
titans.tagline: Proved atoms exist using statistics. Nobody believed him. He was right about everything. The universe literally runs on his equation.
titans.quote: If you are out to describe the truth, leave elegance to the tailor.
titans.quoteContext: A man who cared about being correct, not being pretty about it.
powerMoves: Boltzmann equation — the foundation of statistical mechanics and kinetic theory
S = k ln W — entropy defined. So fundamental it's engraved on his tombstone.
Proved the second law of thermodynamics statistically — entropy always increases, deal with it
Boltzmann distribution — describes how energy distributes in any system at thermal equilibrium
Championed atomic theory — when most physicists thought atoms were a useful fiction
titans.funFact: Was so aggressively right about atoms that the constant stress of being dismissed by the scientific establishment contributed to severe depression. Tragically took his own life in 1906. Three years later, Einstein's Brownian motion paper proved atoms exist beyond all doubt. The universe owed him an apology.
rivalries: Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald (who denied atoms existed — they were wrong, he was right, it cost him everything)

titans.name: Werner Heisenberg
titans.tagline: Proved that certainty itself has limits. When asked where he was, the answer was fundamentally unknowable. (Not a joke. That's the physics.)
titans.quote: What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.
titans.quoteContext: One of the most profound things ever said about the relationship between observer and reality.
powerMoves: Uncertainty principle — you literally cannot know both position and momentum exactly. Not because instruments are bad. Because the universe said no.
Matrix mechanics — invented a complete formulation of quantum mechanics at 23
Won the Nobel at 31 — for 'the creation of quantum mechanics'
S-matrix theory — planted seeds that grew into modern particle physics
Helgoland breakthrough — reimagined all of atomic physics during an allergy retreat on a barren island
titans.funFact: Developed matrix mechanics without knowing what matrices were. When Born pointed out he'd independently invented matrix algebra, Heisenberg was annoyed — he thought matrices were an ugly way to describe his beautiful physics.
tea: Stayed in Nazi Germany during WWII and led their nuclear research program. Whether he deliberately sabotaged the German bomb or simply failed to build one is one of the most debated questions in the history of science. The Farm Hall transcripts — secretly recorded after his capture — show him shocked that the Americans succeeded. Make of that what you will.

After the war, he promoted the narrative that he'd intentionally slowed the German program for moral reasons. His former colleagues, particularly Bohr, disputed this vigorously. The man who proved certainty has limits left the biggest uncertainty of his career: was he a secret hero or just a physicist who got the math wrong?

titans.name: Roger Penrose
titans.tagline: Won the Nobel at 89. Has been correct about black holes since before most physicists were born. Still going.
titans.quote: Intelligence cannot be present without understanding. No computer has any awareness of what it does.
titans.quoteContext: Controversial take from a man whose mathematical work literally enables the computers he's critiquing.
powerMoves: Penrose singularity theorem — proved black holes MUST form under general relativity. Won the Nobel.
Penrose diagrams — mapped the causal structure of spacetime so mortals can draw it on paper
Penrose tiling — aperiodic patterns that tile the plane without repeating. Found in quasicrystals decades later.
Twistor theory — a radical reimagining of spacetime geometry that's still producing results
The Road to Reality — a 1,099-page textbook that starts at basic math and ends at the frontier of physics. Light reading.
titans.funFact: His father was a geneticist, his brother a chess champion, his other brother a mathematician. Sunday dinners must have been insufferable if you weren't a genius.
rivalries: Strong AI proponents (he's been arguing consciousness isn't computable since the 1980s and will not stop)

untouchable.label: The Untouchables
untouchable.subtitle: The final bosses of science. If knowledge were a video game, these are the devs.

absolute-unit.label: Absolute Units
absolute-unit.subtitle: Any one of their contributions would be a career. They had five. Before 30.

built-different.label: Built Different
built-different.subtitle: Saw the rules. Broke them. Were proven right. Some posthumously, which is the ultimate flex.
